'''Erich von Däniken''' (born 1935) is a Swiss author whose 1968 book '''''Chariots of the Gods?''''' launched the modern "'''ancient astronauts'''" idea into global popular culture. He is the central popularizer of the Alienist pole of the [[Alienism vs Angelicalism]] divide, and appears in [[Media and Personalities]] as a thinker whose framework drives a huge swath of ancient-mystery media.

== The thesis ==

Von Däniken's claim is simple and sweeping: many of the achievements and myths of the ancient world are better explained by '''extraterrestrial visitors''' than by the people who left them. The "gods" of ancient religion were spacefaring aliens; monuments such as the pyramids, the Nazca lines, and megalithic sites were built with, or inspired by, their technology; and scripture and myth are garbled eyewitness reports of these encounters. ''Chariots of the Gods?'' sold tens of millions of copies and seeded decades of books, films, and eventually a television franchise.

== The strong case ==

The honest kernel is that the ancient record genuinely contains things that are strange, impressive, and under-appreciated, and von Däniken had a popular writer's gift for making people curious about archaeology, astronomy, and old texts at all. As a gateway to wonder about the deep human past, the work did real cultural work.

== The weak case ==

As archaeology it does not hold up. The arguments lean on an '''argument from incredulity''' ("I can't see how they built this, therefore aliens"), on misread or cherry-picked evidence, and — most seriously — on quietly '''taking credit away from the human beings''', very often non-European peoples, who demonstrably designed and built these monuments. Professional archaeologists classify it as pseudo-archaeology, and the Library treats it the same way: read it as a cultural phenomenon and a spur to curiosity, not as history, and set it against the angelic reading it is usually opposed to in [[Alienism vs Angelicalism]].
